design_rationale: The study explicitly reports random allocation of 175 participants to three arms using an independent statistician-generated sequence with variable block sizes.

domain_judgments.rationale: An independent statistician generated a variable-block random sequence, allocation was implemented through consecutively numbered envelopes handled by researchers uninvolved in collection or intervention, and reported baseline characteristics show no important imbalances.
domain_judgments.evidence_quote: A statistician independent of the research group generated the random allocation, performed in variable block sizes. The random allocation sequences were transferred to consecutively numbered envelopes and were handled by two researchers who were not involved in the data collection or the intervention.

domain_judgments.rationale: Participants necessarily knew whether they received exercise and motivational support, adherence was low, second-year exercise behavior was unmeasured, and the authors used complete-case rather than intention-to-treat analysis, so intervention-related deviations and inappropriate analysis could materially affect the estimated effect.
domain_judgments.evidence_quote: This study did not use intention-to-treat (ITT) analysis, which is commonly used in RCT studies.

domain_judgments.rationale: Only 124 of 175 randomized participants were included in the main 2-year analyses, with differential retention across arms and complete-case analysis; nonsignificant tests of dropout proportions do not establish that missingness was unrelated to outcomes.
domain_judgments.evidence_quote: At the 2-year follow-up, there were dropouts in each group: the OEP group included 38 (62%) of the 61 participants who were included at baseline; the OEP+MI group included 42 participants (72%) of the 58 who were included at baseline; and the control group included 44 (79%) of the 56 participants who were included at baseline.

domain_judgments.rationale: The study used established instruments and common assessment procedures, but it only states that it was single-blinded without identifying who was blinded, while several outcomes were self-reported and participants could not be blinded to behavioral treatment assignment; fall data also mixed calendars with retrospectively reported, imputed categories.
domain_judgments.evidence_quote: The study was performed single blinded.

domain_judgments.rationale: The trial was registered, but the text does not establish a prespecified analysis plan, and numerous outcomes and analytic approaches—including change-score ANOVA, dichotomization, within-group testing, and alternate fall measurements—create scope for selective reporting.
domain_judgments.evidence_quote: The study was registered at clinicaltrials.gov under NCT01778972.

overall_summary: Overall risk of bias is high, driven by substantial and differential missing outcome data analyzed without intention-to-treat and by low adherence/unmeasured postintervention behavior that was not handled with an analysis preserving randomization. Outcome blinding and prespecification of the reported analyses were also insufficiently clear.

design_rationale: This was a cluster-randomized controlled trial in which participating general practices were allocated using a blockwise randomization list prepared by an otherwise uninvolved statistician.

domain_judgments.rationale: Although the GP allocation sequence was generated independently using block randomization, patients were identified and recruited after allocation by GPs and staff who knew their assignment, creating substantial potential for differential recruitment into clusters; allocation concealment before GP assignment was also not explicitly described.
domain_judgments.evidence_quote: After attending the educational workshop, the GPs were randomized either to the intervention or the CG and started to recruit their patients.

domain_judgments.rationale: Participants and care providers were necessarily aware of assignment, possible changes to control practices after the common educational workshop were not evaluated, and the analysis approach was not clearly described as intention-to-treat, although intervention adherence was generally high and no adverse events were reported.
domain_judgments.evidence_quote: Also, we obtained no information about whether the educational session changed the usual care routine of the control GPs.

domain_judgments.rationale: The text provided does not clearly report T1 outcome completeness by randomized group or explain how missing outcome observations were handled, despite noting that some randomized GPs recruited no participants or dropped out.
domain_judgments.evidence_quote: In addition, not all randomized GPs were able to recruit participants or lost interest and therefore dropped out the study.

domain_judgments.rationale: Outcomes were measured consistently with standardized protocols and established instruments, but unblinded GPs or practice staff assessed performance and self-reported outcomes, so knowledge of assignment could plausibly influence measurements, especially stopwatch-based tests and fear-of-falling responses.
domain_judgments.evidence_quote: Neither the GP nor staff members were blinded to the randomization allocation − blinding for the testing procedure is not feasible in an exercise intervention study because participants in the exercise intervention arm would tell their GPs what they were doing.

domain_judgments.rationale: The study had a prospectively registered and previously published protocol, explicitly reports that no protocol changes were made, specifies the four outcomes and group-by-time interaction analysis, and reports both significant and nonsignificant results.
domain_judgments.evidence_quote: The study protocol (PreFalls NCT01032252) we used has been previously published and no changes were made.

overall_summary: Overall risk of bias is high, driven by post-randomization patient recruitment by unblinded cluster personnel and outcome assessment by unblinded GP staff for outcomes susceptible to assessor and participant influence. Unclear outcome-data completeness and possible deviations or contamination add further concerns, despite independent sequence generation and prospective protocol registration.

design_rationale: This was a cluster-randomized trial because the 16 senior centers, rather than individual participants, were explicitly randomly assigned to four intervention conditions.

domain_judgments.rationale: Centers were explicitly randomized, but the sequence-generation and allocation-concealment methods were not reported, and the small number of clusters produced notable differences in group size and sex distribution.
domain_judgments.evidence_quote: The 16 senior centers were randomly assigned to one of the four treatment groups (exercise, cognitive-behavioral, exercise-cognitive, discussion control), and all subjects at a center were given the same intervention.

domain_judgments.rationale: Participants and providers necessarily knew the behavioral condition, intervention contact differed substantially between groups, noncompliance was defined but handling in the primary analysis was not described, and the participant-level analyses did not account for cluster assignment, making the estimated intervention effect potentially biased.
domain_judgments.evidence_quote: The exercise and exercise-cognitive intervention groups met for 1 hour, 3 days per week, for 1 year. The cognitive-behavioral and discussion control intervention groups met for 1 hour, 1 day per week, for 1 year.

domain_judgments.rationale: Overall attrition was 20%, was highest in the cognitive group, and dropouts more often had a prior fall than completers, so missingness could plausibly depend on fall risk despite the reported nonsignificant between-group attrition difference.
domain_judgments.evidence_quote: At the end of the intervention year, attrition of the overall sample was 20%... Thirty-seven percent of the dropouts were previous fallers compared with 27% of those who completed the study.

domain_judgments.rationale: Falls and injury were measured frequently and uniformly with defined procedures, but both were self-reported by participants who knew their assigned intervention, and awareness of a fall-prevention condition could influence reporting.
domain_judgments.evidence_quote: To avoid underreporting, we monitored falls weekly in person or with phone calls and asked for monthly diaries on falls and health status.

domain_judgments.rationale: No preregistration or prespecified statistical analysis plan is reported, while several fall thresholds, time-to-event analyses, fall rates, injury outcomes, and secondary outcomes were available, leaving scope for selective choice among eligible analyses.
domain_judgments.evidence_quote: A log-rank test with time to first fall of events that entailed injury level 4 or greater showed no significant differences among experimental groups.

overall_summary: Overall risk of bias is high, driven principally by concerns in the effect-of-assignment analysis: adherence handling was unclear and participant-level analyses did not account for cluster randomization. Additional concerns arise from incompletely described randomization, 20% attrition, unblinded self-reported outcomes, and lack of a prespecified analysis plan.

design_rationale: This was an explicitly randomized three-arm trial; the first author generated the allocation sequence using a computer-developed random table.

domain_judgments.rationale: The sequence was computer-generated, allocation was concealed from the recruiting assistant, and reported baseline characteristics and outcomes were balanced across groups.
domain_judgments.evidence_quote: The first author used a computer-developed random table to randomly assign patients to three intervention groups: control, CB alone or CB with Tai Chi. Allocation was concealed from the recruiting RA.

domain_judgments.rationale: Participants and intervention providers could not be blinded to these behavioral interventions, and requiring completion of all CB sessions and minimum Tai Chi attendance raises concern about adherence-related deviations, although the reported mixed-model analysis used an intention-to-treat approach including all randomized participants.
domain_judgments.evidence_quote: Participants in this study needed to complete all eight sessions of the CB intervention... Participants in the CB with Tai Chi intervention needed to complete the Tai Chi at least three times a week for 8 weeks, and the CB intervention all eight sessions.

domain_judgments.rationale: Attrition was small (14 of 186), dropouts and completers were reportedly similar at baseline, and mixed models included all randomized participants and accounted for missing follow-up observations.
domain_judgments.evidence_quote: Changes in outcome variables at various follow-up times were predicted using a mixed model approach with an intent-to-treat approach whereby all randomized participants were included, and a mixed model was used to account for missing follow-up data.

domain_judgments.rationale: Validated measures were applied at the same scheduled times by a blinded research assistant, but key outcomes such as fear of falling, falls, social support, and quality of life were participant-reported and could be influenced by participants' unavoidable knowledge of intervention assignment.
domain_judgments.evidence_quote: Participants in all three groups were assessed in their homes for outcomes (see below) at baseline, 2 months, and 5 months by an RA blinded to their group allocation.

domain_judgments.rationale: No preregistration or prespecified statistical analysis plan is reported, while multiple outcomes, subscales, time points, and analyses were available, creating scope for selective reporting despite generally comprehensive tables.
domain_judgments.evidence_quote: The aim of the study was to compare the effectiveness of three interventions (control, CB alone and CB with Tai Chi) on primary outcomes (fear of falling and falls), and secondary outcomes [mobility (gait and balance), social support and quality of life] of community-dwelling elderly adults over 5 months.

overall_summary: Overall risk of bias is judged as some concerns. Randomization, concealment, baseline balance, blinded outcome collection, low attrition, and intention-to-treat mixed modeling were strengths, but lack of participant blinding for subjective outcomes, possible adherence-related deviations, and absence of a preregistered analysis plan leave concerns.

design_rationale: This was a cluster-randomized trial in which senior centers were assigned to SESEP or attention control, with allocation determined using a coin toss.

domain_judgments.rationale: Cluster allocation used a random coin toss and reported baseline comparability, but allocation concealment was not described and participants were recruited after site randomization.
domain_judgments.evidence_quote: A coin was tossed to determine allocation between the Brooklyn sites and the South Bronx/Upper Manhattan sites.

domain_judgments.rationale: Participants and interventionists could not be blinded to the visibly different exercise and nutrition programs, fidelity was incompletely monitored, and the reported complete-case analysis was not intention-to-treat, although no specific intervention-related deviations were documented.
domain_judgments.evidence_quote: While the numbers of participants at each SESEP class were collected, the individual names of attendees were not consistently recorded. In addition, it was not known how much time the individual actually engaged in exercise during the class.

domain_judgments.rationale: Only 62% of randomized participants had follow-up data, reasons for missingness were not obtained, and analysis was restricted to observed follow-up cases, so substantial bias from missing outcomes cannot be excluded.
domain_judgments.evidence_quote: Follow-up testing included 103 participants (62%), 39 from control sites and 64 from treatment sites... There was a significant loss to follow-up with no information obtained as to why the participant did not attend the follow-up screening.

domain_judgments.rationale: Key outcomes, including exercise and physical activity, were interviewer-administered self-reports susceptible to differential reporting because participants knew their intervention, and blinding of interviewers or functional assessors was not reported.
domain_judgments.evidence_quote: In addition to the selective nature of the sample... the outcomes were all based on self-report rather than objective measures of physical activity (e.g., actigraphy).

domain_judgments.rationale: No preregistration or prespecified statistical analysis plan was reported, multiple primary and secondary outcomes were assessed, and the analysis did not appropriately account for the cluster-randomized design, leaving potential for selective choice among analyses.
domain_judgments.evidence_quote: Because there were no statistically significant differences in outcomes based on clusters, no corrections were made for the effects of clustering.

overall_summary: Overall risk of bias is high, driven by substantial unexplained loss to follow-up with complete-case analysis and vulnerable, largely self-reported outcomes measured without reported blinding. Additional concerns include unreported allocation concealment, incomplete fidelity monitoring, lack of intention-to-treat analysis, and no prospective analysis plan.

design_rationale: The investigators explicitly randomized 319 participants within race and living-arrangement strata using random permuted blocks and opaque-envelope allocation.

domain_judgments.rationale: The allocation sequence used stratified random permuted blocks, was implemented with opaque envelopes, and produced groups without important measured baseline imbalances.
domain_judgments.evidence_quote: Study participants were stratified by race (white, nonwhite) and living arrangement (alone, with others) and randomized within each of four strata using random permuted blocks... Randomization lists and four sets of randomization were prepared using double, opaque envelopes.

domain_judgments.rationale: Participants and treating therapists could not be blinded and the no-treatment comparator created a substantial difference in professional attention, although implementation was monitored and analyses included all participants with available outcome data regardless of participation level.
domain_judgments.evidence_quote: Participants who were assigned to the no-treatment control group did not receive any intervention contact... Analyses followed intention to treat such that all subjects providing data were included in analyses regardless of study participation level.

domain_judgments.rationale: Outcome data were available for 94% of randomized participants at 6 months and 89% at 12 months, with attrition reasons reported and no clear evidence of differential missingness by randomized group.
domain_judgments.evidence_quote: Of the 319 participants (159 control, 160 experimental), 300 (94%) were available at 6 months and 285 (89%) at 12 months.

domain_judgments.rationale: Most primary outcomes were subjective self-reports from participants who necessarily knew whether they had received intensive therapist contact, so treatment knowledge and attention could plausibly influence outcome reporting despite masked interviewers; the authors explicitly identify this limitation.
domain_judgments.evidence_quote: One potential limitation of this study was the use of a no-treatment control group, which leaves open the possibility that attention from health professionals may account for the beneficial effects... A related concern is that the primary study outcomes were subjective self-reports of difficulty with daily life tasks and that performance-based measures were not included.

domain_judgments.rationale: No preregistration or prespecified statistical analysis plan is reported, and numerous outcomes, component activities, time points, and covariate-adjusted analyses created scope for selective reporting, although primary and secondary outcome families were identified in the article.
domain_judgments.evidence_quote: Primary outcomes included self-report measures of functional difficulties, self-efficacy, and fear of falling, and secondary outcomes included adaptive strategy use and observed home hazards.

overall_summary: Overall risk of bias is high because the principal outcomes were subjective self-reports from unblinded participants in an intervention-versus-no-treatment comparison, making measurement susceptible to expectancy and attention effects. Randomization and retention were otherwise strong, but lack of prospective registration also raises some concern about selective reporting.

design_rationale: The study explicitly reports computer-generated block randomization performed after baseline measurement by an independent researcher.

domain_judgments.rationale: A computer-generated block-randomization sequence was implemented after baseline by an independent researcher blinded to participant characteristics, and the groups were broadly comparable at baseline.
domain_judgments.evidence_quote: After baseline measurement, an independent researcher blinded to participant characteristics performed block randomization (two communities × 5 cycles) using a computer-generated random allocation (SPSS 12.0, SPSS, Inc., Chicago, IL).

domain_judgments.rationale: Participants could not be blinded and intervention uptake was poor, with 42.1% attending fewer than five sessions; although there was no crossover and available outcomes were analyzed by assigned group, the modified intention-to-treat analysis excluded participants with unavailable follow-up data.
domain_judgments.evidence_quote: Participants were not blinded to group assignment. No participant assigned to the intervention group crossed over to the control group or vice versa... All analyses were performed according to modified intention to treat (i.e., all baseline data and available follow-up data were included).

domain_judgments.rationale: Outcome attrition was substantial and differential (30.0% intervention versus 19.6% control), with no outcome data for those lost and no sensitivity analysis addressing plausible missing-not-at-random mechanisms, so bias from missing outcomes could materially affect the estimates.
domain_judgments.evidence_quote: During the trial, 135 participants were lost to follow-up: 51 (19.6%) of the control group and 84 (30.0%) of the intervention group.

domain_judgments.rationale: Measures were administered consistently and telephone outcome assessors were blinded, but the principal fear and avoidance outcomes were self-reported by participants who necessarily knew their allocation and could therefore have been influenced by the behavioral intervention.
domain_judgments.evidence_quote: Participants were not blinded to group assignment... self-reported data were collected using questionnaires and structured telephone interviews... Outcome assessors were trained centrally on study procedures and were blind to group assignment.

domain_judgments.rationale: The trial was prospectively registered, outcomes and follow-up times were clearly specified, and the paper states that covariate adjustment and per-protocol analyses were prespecified, with results presented across the stated outcomes and time points.
domain_judgments.evidence_quote: Further details of this parallel-group randomized controlled trial (ISRCTN43792817) are available... A priori it was specified that all models would be adjusted for baseline values, age, sex, living situation, educational level, cognitive status, perceived general health, and falls history at baseline.

overall_summary: Overall risk of bias is high because substantial, differential missing outcome data create a high risk of attrition bias. Additional concerns arise from participant awareness of assignment, poor intervention adherence, modified intention-to-treat analysis, and participant-reported outcomes susceptible to expectancy effects.

design_rationale: The paper explicitly reports computerized random allocation by an independent third party with concealment, although randomization occurred separately within two recruitment waves rather than across all four groups.

domain_judgments.rationale: A concealed computerized sequence was used by an independent third party, but allocation was staged by recruitment wave (wave 1 only to CG or MG and wave 2 only to SBG or FG), and statistically significant baseline imbalances in education and fear of falling raise some concern about comparability across the four groups.
domain_judgments.evidence_quote: All randomizations were concealed. (A third party not involved in the study applied a computerized random-number generator.)

domain_judgments.rationale: Participants could not be blinded to exercise versus no intervention, and the analysis was modified intention-to-treat using available follow-up data rather than a full intention-to-treat analysis, although adherence and intervention fidelity were high and no important protocol deviations were reported.
domain_judgments.evidence_quote: All analyses were performed according to a modified intention-to-treat design (i.e., all baseline data and available follow-up data were included).

domain_judgments.rationale: Only 73.9% had complete 24-month data, with 16.8% missing at the 24-month assessment and outcome-specific availability sometimes substantially lower; analyses assumed mixed models were robust without imputation, and limited dropout comparisons did not establish that missingness was unrelated to outcomes.
domain_judgments.evidence_quote: Complete data sets were available for 207 participants (73.9%) for 24 months, and data were missing for 16 persons (5.7%) at 6 months, for 10 persons (3.6%) at 12 months, and for 47 persons (16.8%) at 24 months.

domain_judgments.rationale: Physical-performance outcomes were measured with standardized tests by blinded trained assessors and falls were prospectively recorded, but self-reported psychological outcomes and fall calendars could be influenced by participants' unavoidable knowledge of treatment assignment.
domain_judgments.evidence_quote: The assessors administering the physical performance tests received training and were blinded to group assignment.

domain_judgments.rationale: The models and covariate adjustments were described as specified a priori, but no protocol or prespecified statistical analysis plan is reported, and numerous outcomes, time points, and comparisons permit selective reporting or emphasis.
domain_judgments.evidence_quote: Adjustment of the models for available baseline values of the outcome variables age, sex, living situation, education, fear of falling, and having fallen in the past 6 months was specified a priori.

overall_summary: Overall risk of bias is high, driven primarily by substantial and outcome-specific missing data at long-term follow-up without convincing evidence that missingness could not bias results. Additional concerns arise from wave-restricted randomization, participant awareness and modified intention-to-treat analysis, self-reported outcomes, and lack of a reported protocol or prespecified analysis plan.

design_rationale: The study explicitly randomized 42 eligible participants 1:1 using a computer-generated sequence, with assignment obtained only after baseline assessment.

domain_judgments.rationale: The allocation sequence was computer-generated and held by an independent colleague until baseline assessment was complete; although psychiatric diagnoses differed between groups in this small pilot, the reported method provides no indication that allocation was manipulated.
domain_judgments.evidence_quote: Randomization was determined using a computer-generated sequence created and held by a colleague with no other connection to the study; the project coordinator obtained the assignment after each participant completed the baseline assessment.

domain_judgments.rationale: Participants and providers could not be blinded to these distinct behavioral interventions, one ABLE participant withdrew because of increased anxiety, and adherence was incomplete, although fidelity monitoring and intention-to-treat mixed-model analyses were used.
domain_judgments.evidence_quote: One ABLE participant dropped out because of increased anxiety and one did not provide a reason... Intention-to-treat analyses were conducted using repeated measures mixed effects models.

domain_judgments.rationale: Outcome follow-up was available for 40 of 42 randomized participants (95.2%), with both losses in ABLE, and mixed-effects models retained observations in the presence of missing data, making material bias unlikely.
domain_judgments.evidence_quote: Two participants dropped out of ABLE (9.5%) after 4 weeks. A total of 40 participants completed treatment and follow-up.

domain_judgments.rationale: The validated FES-I and activity measure were administered consistently by blinded research associates, but the principal outcomes were participant-reported and participants necessarily knew their intervention, which could influence reports; the modified Activity Card Sort also lacked reported validation for this use.
domain_judgments.evidence_quote: All assessments were completed by research associates blind to the participants’ treatment condition.

domain_judgments.rationale: The trial was registered and the primary outcomes were identified, but the manuscript does not establish that outcomes and analyses were prospectively specified before unblinded data were available, and it reports multiple time-point and acute/follow-up analyses.
domain_judgments.evidence_quote: All procedures were approved by the local Institutional Review Board and the trial was registered with the National Institutes of Health clinical trials registry (NCT01609322).

overall_summary: Overall risk of bias is some concerns. Randomization and retention were strong, but lack of participant blinding for subjective outcomes, possible intervention-related deviations, and insufficient evidence that all reported analyses were prospectively specified prevent a low-risk judgment.

design_rationale: Participants were explicitly randomized after baseline assessment using a predetermined block-randomization list prepared by an independent statistician.

domain_judgments.rationale: The sequence was independently generated with variable block sizes and observed baseline characteristics were broadly balanced, but the report does not clearly describe how the allocation list was concealed from recruiters and enrolling personnel until assignment.
domain_judgments.evidence_quote: A predetermined randomisation list was made by an independent statistician. Randomisation was performed in blocks to minimise the risk of revealing treatment group membership, with a variable size of three, six, nine or twelve participants.

domain_judgments.rationale: Participants and treating physiotherapists could not be blinded, intervention delivery had fidelity limitations, and only 73% reportedly exercised as planned, although the reported obstacles were largely health or contextual factors and there is no clear evidence of outcome-impacting co-interventions.
domain_judgments.evidence_quote: Exercises that were performed as planned were rated as ‘yes’ in 73% of the questionnaires, and the comments addressing this included health-related issues, e.g., illness, pain and hospitalisation, lack of motivation and external factors, e.g., weather.

domain_judgments.rationale: Three-month outcomes were available for 40 of 45 randomized participants (89%), with somewhat greater apparent attrition in the intervention groups, and no reasons-for-missingness analysis or sensitivity analysis was reported.
domain_judgments.evidence_quote: Three-month follow-ups were conducted for 40 participants.

domain_judgments.rationale: Validated physical-performance and self-efficacy measures were applied across groups by nominally blinded independent physiotherapists, but falls and FES were participant-reported in an unblinded behavioral trial and assessor blinding success was not documented.
domain_judgments.evidence_quote: All measurements were completed in the participant's home or at a health care centre formed by an independent PT who was blinded for group randomisation.

domain_judgments.rationale: No preregistered analysis plan is reported, and the paper evaluates several outcomes with multiple between-group and within-group analyses while emphasizing nominally significant within-group findings despite nonsignificant between-group effects, creating substantial risk of selective result reporting.
domain_judgments.evidence_quote: No significant differences between the groups were observed over time. Within groups, the median (min–max) fall-related self-efficacy for the MI group was 97.5 points (60–130), and this value improved significantly (p = 0.02, ES (r) = 0.45) to 124 points (91–130) at the three-month follow-up.

overall_summary: Overall risk of bias is high, driven primarily by substantial risk of selective reporting from multiple outcomes and analytic contrasts without a reported prespecified analysis plan, including emphasis on within-group significance when between-group effects were nonsignificant. Additional concerns arise from unclear allocation concealment, intervention nonadherence/fidelity limitations, modest and unexplained attrition, and participant-reported outcomes in an unblinded trial.

design_rationale: Participants were explicitly randomly allocated to three groups using variable block randomization stratified by community, with the sequence generated by an independent statistician.

domain_judgments.rationale: The sequence was appropriately generated independently and baseline groups were similar, but allocation concealment is not fully assured because the report does not state that the consecutively numbered envelopes were opaque and sealed.
domain_judgments.evidence_quote: A statistician independent from the research group generated the random allocation. The random allocation sequences were transferred to consecutively numbered envelopes that were handled by 2 researchers who did not participate in the data collection or in the intervention.

domain_judgments.rationale: Participants and treating physiotherapists necessarily knew the behavioral/exercise assignment, and although fidelity was monitored and an intention-to-treat analysis was reported, the analyzed ITT population excluded participants without follow-up data and the control group's exercise behavior was unknown.
domain_judgments.evidence_quote: The control group did not keep exercise diaries, so it is unknown whether this group exercised on their own.

domain_judgments.rationale: Outcome data were unavailable for 14 of 175 randomized participants (8%), mostly because of health problems, and no sensitivity analysis or evidence was provided to establish that missingness could not bias the results.
domain_judgments.evidence_quote: A total of 161 participants were followed up at 12 weeks... The 14 dropouts during the study period were mostly due to participants’ health-related problems.

domain_judgments.rationale: The outcomes were measured with established instruments or prospective calendars/diaries using common procedures, and independent physiotherapists assessing performance outcomes were blinded to allocation; although some outcomes were self-reported and participants could not be blinded, this is unlikely to create major differential measurement bias across the broad outcome set.
domain_judgments.evidence_quote: The measurements were performed single blinded by 6 independent PTs before randomization and 12 weeks after randomization.

domain_judgments.rationale: The trial was registered and the primary outcome and analyses were described, but the provided report does not establish a prespecified analysis plan and reports numerous outcomes, ITT/per-protocol analyses, and within-group tests, leaving potential analytic multiplicity and selective emphasis.
domain_judgments.evidence_quote: The study was registered at clinicaltrials.gov under NCT01778972.

overall_summary: Overall risk of bias is judged as some concerns. This is driven by incomplete reporting of envelope concealment, nonblinding and uncertain control-group activity, 8% missing follow-up data without a missingness analysis, and potential selective reporting from multiple outcomes and analyses; blinded outcome assessment and generally balanced baseline groups reduce concern.

design_rationale: Participants were explicitly allocated by computerized stratified two-block randomization to intervention or control, conducted by an external agency after baseline measurement.

domain_judgments.rationale: The allocation sequence was computerized and stratified, allocation was performed externally after baseline assessment, and reported baseline characteristics were broadly comparable.
domain_judgments.evidence_quote: A computerized two-block randomization was performed using the level of concerns about falls ... as the prognostic factor. An external agency blinded to participant characteristics conducted the randomization directly after the baseline measurement.

domain_judgments.rationale: Participants and facilitators were unblinded, 15% of intervention participants never started and a further 29% of starters withdrew, indicating substantial nonadherence, although the primary analysis followed intention-to-treat and no crossover was permitted.
domain_judgments.evidence_quote: Cross-over between groups was not permitted, and participants were aware of their group allocation. ... Thirty participants in the intervention group (15 %) were not exposed to the program; they withdrew from the intervention prior to the first session. Among the people who started the program, 29 % (47 out of 164) withdrew.

domain_judgments.rationale: Outcome attrition was substantial and differential (about 17% control versus 31–34% intervention), with reasons such as health problems and perceived burden plausibly related to outcomes and intervention experience; multiple imputation at the scale level does not fully resolve bias from participants lacking sufficient follow-up.
domain_judgments.evidence_quote: The dropout rates during the trial were 17 % (n = 33) in the control and 31 % (n = 61) in the intervention group. ... Therefore selective dropout may be an issue.

domain_judgments.rationale: Validated and consistently administered measures were used and interview assessors were blinded, but the primary and several secondary outcomes were participant-reported and could be influenced by participants' knowledge of allocation in this behavioral trial.
domain_judgments.evidence_quote: Facilitators and participants were aware of group assignments; outcome assessors were blinded to the allocation.

domain_judgments.rationale: The trial was prospectively registered, a published protocol identified the outcomes and planned analyses, and the paper reports outcomes at both prespecified follow-up times, leaving little indication of selective result reporting.
domain_judgments.evidence_quote: Trial registration: ClinicalTrials.gov, NCT01358032. Registered 17 May 2011 ... Additional information about the study design can be found in a published study protocol.

overall_summary: Overall risk of bias is high because substantial, differential attrition creates a serious possibility that missing outcomes biased the estimated intervention effect. Additional concerns arise from intervention nonadherence and unblinded participant-reported outcomes, despite sound randomization, blinded interview assessors, intention-to-treat analysis, and prospective registration.
